This makes me think that it's likely a combination of pheromones and the physical act of mating that is driving the behaviour. So, I wonder how relevant it is to look for representation of cVA with the identified circuit elements -for example in the B1 DANs. Assessing the representation of the polyamine in a mating dependent way might be more relevant (and the authors have done this for many of their experiments).

Was there a reason why the authors decided to use an of 16 for the single fly experiments?

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

For a previous review I had asked some things, for example if exposure to cVA alone induces preference. I am quite happy to see these experiments now included in the new version of the paper, although it seems a coincidence that I am asked to review another time.

I think the paper has improved and it is also easier to read now.

Since I reviewed before, and my comments were seemingly already incorporated, I don't have so many new comments!

Suggestions:

1) line 151 following, Figure 1 C, D > I don't understand why these response to cVA experiments are shown here and how they fit with the natural flow of the story- just take them out? It is an interesting finding on its own but confuses the main story a bit. After all, the paper deals with the response to polyamine and how that changes after mating.

2) Figure 6 A: replace red green color scheme with one more suitable for red green blind.

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

Although the amount of data is impressive, it obscures main conclusions. Trim them to minimal set of data to support the main conclusions. For instance, data in Figure 3C and 3D are irrelevant to the model in Figure 7. Also some of data seem to be replication of previous reports and dispensable. For instance, Figure 1C-D are replication of Siju et al., 2020. ovoD1 mutant data was in Hussain et al., 2016. Otherwise, please clarify what is novel about these data. Along the same line, there is only weak link between data of Kenyon cells and LHON (Figure 2 and 6) and PAM-b'1/MBON-b'1.

[Editors’ note: further revisions were suggested prior to acceptance, as described below.]

Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "A dopamine-gated learning circuit underpins reproductive state-dependent odor preference in Drosophila females" for further consideration by eLife. Your revised article has been evaluated by K VijayRaghavan (Senior Editor) and a Reviewing Editor.

The manuscript has been improved, and the reviewers are enthusiastic about its publication provided the following issues, as outlined below, are addressed.

The reviewers appreciate that the authors do not want to trim the data down as was recommended in the initial set of essential revisions. In this case, we are concerned about the specificity of the odour responses for many of the manipulations. However, to keep revisions to the minimum at this stage, our recommendations are the following:

1. Please move the recall experiments (Figure 3E, 3F, 4D, 4F , Figure 7—figure supplement 1) to supplementary data and discuss these in the "ideas and speculation" section. While doing so, do please explicitly state that it is possible that these manipulations might affect response to other odours, which has not been tested.

2. In the imaging data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 we were concerned that the retinal minus control was actually activating DANs (perhaps through the contents of the cornmeal media). Could the authors please test that B'1 DANs are not actually active in their no retinal control by conducting the experiment in the absence of CsChrimson.

The detailed reviews are appended below.

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

In the revised version of the manuscript "A dopamine-gated learning circuit underpins reproductive state-dependent odor preference in Drosophila females », the authors addressed all comments and concerns raised by the reviewers. The manuscript still tells a complex story with some open ends that requires focus and concentration from the reader, but efforts have been made to make the data more accessible than in the first version.

It is helpful that the author inserted a short paragraph with an overview of the olfactory system to the introduction. Other adjustments to the text, e.g. in the discussion, also improved the manuscript.

Figure 1 is more streamlined now.

All requested experiments were carried out. Whenever the requested experiments did not give conclusive results due to supposed technical problems, this was explained in an appropriate way.

From my side, I accept and respect the author's argument that they would not like to completely omit all experiments addressing recall (as was suggested in order to simplify the manuscript).

The new results of LHAD1b2 changing its response to putrescine upon mating (Figure 7) is an interesting finding adding to the story.

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

As shown by the authors, a key feature of mating-induced change of odor preference is its specificity to polyamine. In this study, the authors presented many data that manipulation of some mushroom body cell types enhance or disrupt behavioral response to polyamine. However, such outcome of circuit manipulation does not necessarily mean that those cell types are responsible for induction or expression of polyamine-preference after mating. It could be because circuit manipulation recapitulated a situation after olfactory learning and affected response to arbitral odors including polyamine. Thus, in my opinion, the results of circuit manipulation are uninterpretable without control experiments to test polyamine-specificity (i.e. ammonia for virgin females and vinegar or other attractive odor for mated females).

For MBON-β′1, authors collected new data to show that its thermogenetic activation in virgin females induce long-lasting preference to polyamine but not to ammonia (Figure 4—figure supplement 1). Taken together with blocking experiments (Figure 4A), I'm convinced that MBON-β′1 plays an essential role in duction of mating-induced polyamine preference. I think the data about MBON-β′1 alone is worth publishing. I very much appreciate author's efforts to collect a large amount of data. However, showing them without control experiments about odor-specificity will be confusing to readers and even harmful to future investigation.

I suggested this experiment to establish functional connection between PAM-β′1 and MBON-β′1 either through direct DAN-to-MBON connection as depicted as an arrow in author's model in Figure 8, or through indirect connections. The outcome of DAN activation can be modulatory, but the data in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A showed no evidence of mating-induced or DAN-activation-induced plasticity in the β′1 compartment. Therefore, I postulated that PAM-β′1 may directly activate MBON-β′1, as shown in other compartments (Takemura et al., 2017 eLife), to induce plasticity somewhere else.

The new imaging data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B is hard to interpret without validation of retinal minus control. Without supplement of all-trans-retinal, cornmeal may contain enough precursor for biosynthesis of all-trans-retinal. Thus, to interpret the data, authors need to demonstrate that DANs are not activated by red light in retinal minus control or repeat the experiment without CsChrimson expression. I suspect that clear MBON-β′1 response to red light is due to activation of PAM-β′1 rather than visual response, especially when duration of activation is prolonged. Unlike γ dorsal Kenyon cells, there is no EM connectome data to support visual inputs to the α prime/β prime Kenyon cells.

If PAM-β′1 activation does not activate MBON-β′1, authors need to clarify, at lease in a working model, which synapses are modulated by PAM-β′1.

This new MB057B>dTrpA1 data about polyamine specificity of activation phenotype is a valuable addition. For MBON-β′1, there are a compelling set of data to conclude that MBON-β′1 is required during mating and its activity replace mating experience.

The data to demonstrate ployamine-specificity of the MB188B>dTrpA1 is still missing. I find it essential, especially because blocking PAM-DANs with MB188B>Shi during mating did not show any defect in mating-induced polyamine-preference. If 24-hour activation of DANs with MB188B>dTrpA1 change preference of other odors, it should be considered as artifact of long thermogenetic activation rather than recapitulation of mating experience.

I agree that Figure 2 "during mating" data is not expected and can be a strong result if authors could show polyamine-specificity of Kenon cell perturbation and evidence of mating-induced plasticity inside the mushroom body that is read out during odor test. I suggested to omit the Figure 2 data because the former requires additional experiments, and the latter is not supported by the presented data (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).

To keep the Figure 2 data as a main figure, the vinegar (or other innately attractive odor in both virgins and mated females) should be used as a control odor to distinguish whether the defect of polyamine-preference by circuit-perturbation is due to impairment of forming/expressing mating-induced change or general defect in odor attraction as reported in Wang et al., 2003. As authors noted, a couple of papers claimed that KC's output is dispensable during training for olfactory conditioning. However, the timescale of manipulation is totally different. In the cited olfactory learning papers about short-term memories, temperature was elevated ~30min prior to the training and shifted lower to the permissive temperature immediately after training. In contrast, flies were kept at restrictive temperature for 24 hours in Figure 2 experiments, which likely include a long period after mating.

I suggest validating that mated MB010B>shi flies show intact vinegar attraction compared to control genotypes when temperature is elevated 24-hour period during/around mating or before/during test. Otherwise, I suggest omitting Figure 2 data.

As side notes about olfactory learning literatures, Krashes et al., 2008 Neuron showed that blocking α prime/β prime Kenyon cells impair memory, presumably because KCs are kept inactive for a while after temperature shift. Ichinose et al., 2015 eLife showed that output from the α/β KCs is necessary during training for long-term appetitive memory.

MB188>CsChrimson may not have such problem. I think that author's decision to tone down the conclusion is reasonable.

claims.claim: Hunger increases the sensitivity of sweet taste neurons and quenches that of bitter taste neurons in different animal species including humans.

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Carnell et al., 2012; Chu et al., 2014; LeDue et al., 2016; Palouzier-Paulignan et al., 2012; Rolls, 2007).

claims.claim: The estrous cycle influences how a female mouse perceives a putative mate.

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Dey et al., 2015).

claims.claim: Outside of estrus, the hormone progesterone strongly inhibits the female mouse's male pheromone-sensitive olfactory sensory neurons.
claims.source: Outside of estrus, the hormone progesterone strongly inhibits the female's male pheromone-sensitive olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs), and thereby, completely blunts her interest in males.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about hormonal modulation of sensory neurons.

claims.claim: Polyamines play essential and conserved roles in DNA replication, cell proliferation, embryonic development and healthy aging.
claims.source: Polyamines, namely putrescine, spermine, and spermidine, play essential and conserved roles in most eukaryotic cells and organisms, ranging from DNA replication, cell proliferation, embryonic development to healthy aging (Miller-Fleming et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Miller-Fleming et al., 2015).

claims.claim: High concentrations of putrescine in food increase egg laying in Drosophila females.
claims.source: High concentrations of putrescine in food increase egg laying in Drosophila females (Hussain et al., 2016b).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Hussain et al., 2016b).

claims.claim: Within the first several hours after mating, the expression of sex peptide receptor increases by tenfold in polyamine-detecting olfactory sensory neurons.
claims.source: Within the first several hours after mating, the expression of the neuropeptide receptor, sex peptide receptor (SPR), increases by tenfold in the OSNs leading, when bound to its ligand myoinhibitory peptide (MIP), to a depression of polyamine OSN presynaptic output to the second order neurons of the olfactory system (Hussain et al., 2016a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Hussain et al., 2016a).

claims.claim: Virgin flies show high attraction toward low concentration of polyamines.
claims.source: While virgin flies show a high attraction toward low concentration of polyamines, mated flies are attracted to higher concentrations (Hussain et al., 2016a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Hussain et al., 2016a).

claims.claim: Mated flies are attracted to higher concentrations of polyamines.
claims.source: While virgin flies show a high attraction toward low concentration of polyamines, mated flies are attracted to higher concentrations (Hussain et al., 2016a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Hussain et al., 2016a).

claims.claim: Dopaminergic neurons innervating the mushroom body form neuromodulatory synapses with mushroom body output neurons and Kenyon cells.
claims.source: In particular, the role of dopaminergic neurons (DANs) innervating the 15 compartments of the MB, where they form neuromodulatory synapses with MBONs and the MB intrinsic neurons, the Kenyon cells (KC), have been studied extensively for their role in aversive and appetitive memory formation (Cognigni et al., 2018; Owald and Waddell, 2015; Siju et al., 2021; Thum and Gerber, 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Cognigni et al., 2018; Owald and Waddell, 2015; Siju et al., 2021; Thum and Gerber, 2019).

claims.claim: Dopaminergic neurons respond to contextual information such as reward or punishment and modulate the synapse between mushroom body output neurons and Kenyon cells.
claims.source: In a simple model, DANs respond to contextual information such as reward or punishment and thereby modulate the synapse between a specific MBON, usually of the same compartment as the DAN, and the KCs.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established models of mushroom body function in learning and memory.

claims.claim: Most studies have reported a depression of the Kenyon cell-mushroom body output neuron synapse as a result of context or experience.
claims.source: Most studies have reported a depression of the KC-MBON synapse as a result of context or experience (Cohn et al., 2015; Lewis et al., 2015; Owald et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Cohn et al., 2015; Lewis et al., 2015; Owald et al., 2015).

claims.claim: Dopaminergic neurons might not only modulate mushroom body output neurons but also activate them directly.
claims.source: Further evidence indicates that DANs might not only modulate MBONs but also activate them directly (Takemura et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Takemura et al., 2017).

claims.claim: Learning modulates the response of specific lateral horn output neurons through a mushroom body output neuron connecting the mushroom body to the lateral horn.
claims.source: Dolan et al. recently reported that learning modulates the response of specific LHONs through an MBON connecting the MB to the LH (Dolan et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Dolan et al., 2018).

claims.claim: Innate olfactory behavior is thought to rely on stereotyped circuits connecting specific glomeruli in the antennal lobe to specific neurons in the lateral horn.
claims.source: Innate olfactory behavior is thought to rely on stereotyped circuits connecting specific glomeruli in the AL to specific neurons in the LH (Chin et al., 2018; Ebrahim et al., 2015; Min et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Chin et al., 2018; Ebrahim et al., 2015; Min et al., 2013).

claims.claim: Previous work has implicated the lateral horn in the control of reproductive behaviors, such as responses to sex pheromones.
claims.source: In line with this, previous work in the fly has implicated the LH in the control of reproductive behaviors, such as responses to sex pheromones (Jefferis et al., 2007; Ruta et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Jefferis et al., 2007; Ruta et al., 2010).

claims.claim: Neurons innervating or providing output of the lateral horn show largely stereotypic responses to groups of odors.
claims.source: Neurons innervating or providing output of the LH show largely stereotypic responses to groups of odors (; Jeanne et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Jeanne et al., 2018).

claims.claim: Recent studies implicated neurons in the lateral horn in innate valence decisions and odor classification.
claims.source: Moreover, recent studies implicated neurons in the LH in innate valence decisions and odor classification (Dolan et al., 2019; Jeanne et al., 2018; Strutz et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Dolan et al., 2019; Jeanne et al., 2018; Strutz et al., 2014).

claims.claim: Modulation of innate behavior in the context of hunger involves the mushroom body.
claims.source: Interestingly, modulation of innate behavior, for instance in the context of hunger, also involves the MB (Bräcker et al., 2013; Cohn et al., 2015; Grunwald Kadow, 2018; Heisenberg, 2003; Krashes et al., 2009; Lewis et al., 2015; Sayin et al., 2018; Tsao et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Bräcker et al., 2013; Cohn et al., 2015; Grunwald Kadow, 2018; Heisenberg, 2003; Krashes et al., 2009; Lewis et al., 2015; Sayin et al., 2018; Tsao et al., 2018).

claims.claim: Specific dopaminergic neurons relay the experience of mating to the female's mushroom body, thereby inducing a long-lasting change in female olfactory preference.
claims.source: Our combined data suggest that specific dopaminergic neurons relay the experience of mating to the female's MB, thereby inducing a long-lasting change in female olfactory preference.
claims.evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental data presented in the study.

claims.claim: Mating experience, through the sensation of mating-related odors such as cVA, is relayed to the mushroom body via specific dopaminergic neurons innervating the β'1 compartment.
claims.source: We propose a model wherein mating experience, through the sensation of mating-related odors such as cVA, is relayed to the MB via specific DANs innervating the β'1 compartment.
claims.evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claims.claim: Mating-related stimuli modulate or activate the output of β'1 mushroom body compartment and lastingly change the polyamine response of lateral horn output neuron AD1b2.
claims.source: Thereby, mating-related stimuli modulate or activate the output of β'1, and lastingly change the polyamine response of LHON AD1b2.
claims.evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claims.claim: The expression of higher polyamine preference relies on β'2 mushroom body output neurons and AD1b2 lateral horn output neurons.
claims.source: The expression of this higher preference relies on β'2 MBONs and AD1b2 LHONs, analogous to the situation found upon associative learning (Dolan et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on the experimental data presented in the study and citation to previous work (Dolan et al., 2018).

claims.claim: Changes induced by the experience of mating are induced and expressed through a dopamine-gated learning circuit.
claims.source: Thus, changes induced by the experience of mating are induced and expressed through a dopamine-gated learning circuit.
claims.evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental data presented in the study.

claims.claim: Neither mushroom body output neurons nor lateral horn output neurons are selective for any one odor.
claims.source: Given that neither MBONs nor LHONs are selective for any one odor, we propose that this mechanism could also play a role in the mating state-dependent adaptation of other choice behaviors.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the response properties of these neurons.

claims.claim: The mechanism described could play a role in the mating state-dependent adaptation of other choice behaviors.
claims.source: Given that neither MBONs nor LHONs are selective for any one odor, we propose that this mechanism could also play a role in the mating state-dependent adaptation of other choice behaviors.
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculative proposal based on the experimental findings and known properties of the neurons.

claims.claim: Courtship promoting signals such as the pheromone cVA contribute to a switch in preference behavior during mating.
claims.source: These results provide evidence that courtship promoting signals such as the pheromone cVA contribute to a switch in preference behavior during mating, but that the presence of food odor, including polyamines, during mating is not required.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claims.claim: The presence of food odor, including polyamines, during mating is not required for the switch in preference behavior.
claims.source: These results provide evidence that courtship promoting signals such as the pheromone cVA contribute to a switch in preference behavior during mating, but that the presence of food odor, including polyamines, during mating is not required.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claims.claim: Kenyon cell output is required at two timepoints: to induce the change in behavior upon mating and to influence the expression of the actual behavioral choice.
claims.source: Thus, KC synaptic output appears to be required at two timepoints: First, it is necessary to induce the change in behavior upon mating, and second, it influences the expression of the actual behavioral choice.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claims.claim: PAM dopaminergic neurons promote the expression of mated female odor attraction.
claims.source: These results are consistent with the interpretation that DANs regulate the expression of female odor attraction in a mating state-dependent manner; although PAM-DANs appear to be necessary for the expression of attraction of mated females, the activity of PPL1-DANs in virgins seems to suppress the expression of odor attraction.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claims.claim: PPL1 dopaminergic neurons suppress the expression of odor attraction in virgins.
claims.source: These results are consistent with the interpretation that DANs regulate the expression of female odor attraction in a mating state-dependent manner; although PAM-DANs appear to be necessary for the expression of attraction of mated females, the activity of PPL1-DANs in virgins seems to suppress the expression of odor attraction.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claims.claim: MBON-β'1 synaptic output critically contributes to the induction of mating-related behavioral changes.
claims.source: Blocking of synaptic output of MBON-β'1 during the 24 hr period around mating resulted in a strong reduction of polyamine odor preference in mated females at the time of odor test (Figure 4A). suggesting that this MBON's synaptic output critically contributes to the induction of mating-related behavioral changes.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: At the time of mating, MBON-β'1 and dopaminergic neurons innervating the same compartment modulate the degree of polyamine attraction.
claims.source: Together, these results provide evidence that, at the time of mating, MBON-β'1 and DANs innervating the same compartment modulate the degree of polyamine attraction.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claims.claim: β'2 mushroom body output neuron output is important for the expression of the choice in mated females.
claims.source: These data suggest that β'2 output is important for the expression of the choice in mated females, but in contrast to β'1 output, it is insufficient to induce the mating-induced change in choice behavior.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claims.claim: β'2 mushroom body output neuron output is insufficient to induce the mating-induced change in choice behavior.
claims.source: These data suggest that β'2 output is important for the expression of the choice in mated females, but in contrast to β'1 output, it is insufficient to induce the mating-induced change in choice behavior.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The β'1 compartment provides a contextual signal conveyed to the mushroom body through the experience of mating.
claims.source: We thus propose a similar scenario as observed for learning with the experience of mating providing a contextual signal conveyed to the MB primarily through the β'1 compartment.
claims.evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claims.claim: The β'2 compartment is necessary to express attraction at the time the mating-induced preference is needed.
claims.source: The β'2 compartment, like in expression of learned behavior, is only necessary to express attraction at the time the mating-induced preference is needed.
claims.evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claims.claim: Multiple lateral horn output neurons are involved in the mated female's attraction to polyamines.
claims.source: Altogether, these data indicate that multiple LHONs are involved in the mated female's attraction to polyamines, including AD1b2, which receives strong synaptic input by one type of VC5 PN, and aSP-g neurons, which are activated by cVA as well as some other odors (Kohl et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 5 and citation to previous work (Kohl et al., 2013).

claims.claim: aSP-g neurons are activated by cVA as well as some other odors.
claims.source: Altogether, these data indicate that multiple LHONs are involved in the mated female's attraction to polyamines, including AD1b2, which receives strong synaptic input by one type of VC5 PN, and aSP-g neurons, which are activated by cVA as well as some other odors (Kohl et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Kohl et al., 2013).

claims.claim: Mating does not lead to a long-lasting modulation of MBON-β'1 response to cVA.
claims.source: These data showed that β'1 MBONs respond to cVA and that mating does not lead to a long-lasting modulation of this response.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the calcium imaging data presented in Figure 6.

claims.claim: It is possible that mating leads to a transient, short-lasting plasticity in odor response of MBON-β'1 that was missed during recordings.
claims.source: It is possible, however, that mating leads to a transient, short-lasting plasticity in odor response that we missed during our recordings.
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculative explanation for the lack of observed long-lasting changes.

claims.claim: The bidirectional role of β'1 mushroom body output neurons suggests their modulation by dopaminergic neurons might be complex and not detectable through calcium imaging.
claims.source: In addition, the fact that β'1-MBONs bidirectionally modulate the behavior of virgin and mated females suggests that their role and thus the way they are modulated by DANs might be more complex and not detectable through calcium imaging.
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculative explanation for the lack of observed changes in calcium imaging.

claims.claim: Neurons downstream of the mushroom body involved in the expression of behavior could be lastingly modulated by mating.
claims.source: Second, it is possible that neurons downstream of the MB involved in the expression of the behavior are lastingly modulated.
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculative hypothesis based on the experimental findings.

claims.claim: Mating-induced modulation of the lateral horn is important for female reproductive behavior.
claims.source: These data provide evidence that AD1b2 LHONs are lastingly modulated by mating. This modulation and our finding that they are involved in the expression of putrescine attraction in mated females indicates that mating-induced modulation of the LH is important for female reproductive behavior.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 7.

claims.claim: A mating-induced modulation of mushroom body dopaminergic neurons could be relayed to the lateral horn through MBON-α2sc.
claims.source: Inhibition of MBON-α2sc, which connects the MB to specific neurons in the LH, reduces polyamine attraction in mated females (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) consistent with the hypothesis that a mating-induced modulation of MB DANs could be relayed to the LH.
claims.evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the experimental data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The transition from a sexually immature to a mature, reproducing parent is a major step in the life of most animals.
claims.source: The transition from a sexually immature to a mature, reproducing parent is a major step in the life of most animals.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on general biological knowledge.

claims.claim: Sexual and parental behavior is highly flexible and changes through physiology and with experience.
claims.source: While many aspects of reproductive behavior are innate, sexual and parental behavior is highly flexible and changes through physiology and with experience (Griffith and Ejima, 2009; Koch and Ehret, 1989; Marlin et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Griffith and Ejima, 2009; Koch and Ehret, 1989; Marlin et al., 2015).

claims.claim: Some behavioral and neuronal changes induced by reproductive maturation persist for a significant fraction of an animal's lifespan.
claims.source: In addition, sexually mature animals spend a major proportion of their lives with generating or caring for their offspring. In line with this, some of the behavioral and neuronal changes persist for a significant fraction of an animal's lifespan (Hoekzema et al., 2017; Insel et al., 1995; Reisenman et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Hoekzema et al., 2017; Insel et al., 1995; Reisenman et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2017).

claims.claim: Pheromones are present in the female's environment just before, during and sometime after mating.
claims.source: Of note, males transfer some of their pheromone onto the female during copulation (Keleman et al., 2012), and they also mark feeding and oviposition sites for females by depositing pheromone (Lin et al., 2015), suggesting that pheromones are present in the female's environment just before, during and sometime after mating (Ejima et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Keleman et al., 2012; Lin et al., 2015; Ejima et al., 2007).

claims.claim: The pheromone cVA activates dopaminergic neurons of the β'1 compartment in a mating state-dependent manner.
claims.source: In line with a putative role of odors such as pheromones, in vivo calcium imaging data shows that the pheromone cVA activates DANs of the β'1 compartment; this activation is modulated by state (Siju et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Siju et al., 2020).

claims.claim: The mechanisms described might represent a female version of male courtship learning.
claims.source: We speculate, that the mechanisms we describe here might represent a female version of male courtship learning (Ejima et al., 2007; Keleman et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculative proposal based on the experimental findings and citations to previous work (Ejima et al., 2007; Keleman et al., 2012).

claims.claim: Specific dopaminergic neurons can mimic courtship experience in naive males in the absence of an actual rejection by an already mated female.
claims.source: Consistent with our observations, specific DANs can mimic courtship experience in naive males in the absence of an actual rejection by an already mated female (Keleman et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Keleman et al., 2012).

claims.claim: Males likely associate cVA with the experience of rejection by an already mated female.
claims.source: Males likely associate cVA, which was transferred during previous copulation by another male onto the female, with the experience of rejection by an already mated female (Ejima et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Ejima et al., 2007).

claims.claim: Mating stimulates mechanosensory neurons in the female's reproductive tract and contributes to a switch in her behavior.
claims.source: Naturally, mating itself stimulates also mechanosensory neurons in the female's reproductive tract and thereby appears to contribute to a switch in her behavior (Gou et al., 2014; Shao et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Gou et al., 2014; Shao et al., 2019).

claims.claim: Juvenile hormone drives network maturation of the mushroom body in young flies and promotes their ability to form memories.
claims.source: For instance, JH drives network maturation of the MB in young flies and thereby promotes their ability to form memories (Leinwand and Scott, 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Leinwand and Scott, 2021).

claims.claim: Mating triggers neuropeptide Bursicon release from enteroendocrine cells, which modulates female appetite.
claims.source: Recent elegant work showed that mating triggers neuropeptide (i.e. Bursicon) release from enteroendocrine cells, which in turn modulate female appetite (Hadjieconomou et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Hadjieconomou et al., 2020).

claims.claim: Additional factors beyond pheromones are likely involved in conveying mating experience to the female's higher brain centers.
claims.source: Thus, additional factors are likely involved in conveying mating experience to the female's higher brain centers.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental findings showing that PAM-β'1,γ3/4 inhibition during mating does not prevent the behavioral switch.

claims.claim: PAM-β'1,γ3/4 is sufficient to induce a behavior in a virgin female that resembles a specific aspect of the behavior of a mated female, but it is not strictly necessary.
claims.source: Thus, PAM-β'1,γ3/4 is sufficient to induce a behavior in a virgin female that resembles a specific aspect of the behavior of a mated female, but it not strictly necessary.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claims.claim: Multiple parallel systems ensure the transition from a virgin to a mated female.
claims.source: Given the importance of reproductive behavior for any species, it might not be surprising that multiple parallel systems ensure the transition from a virgin to a mated female.
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation based on the experimental findings.

claims.claim: Previous results using associative learning paradigms suggested that Kenyon cells are not essential during learning but only during test.
claims.source: Previous results using associative learning paradigms suggested that KCs are not essential during learning but only during test (Dubnau et al., 2001; McGuire et al., 2001; Schwaerzel et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Dubnau et al., 2001; McGuire et al., 2001; Schwaerzel et al., 2002).

claims.claim: A recent study suggests that Kenyon cell output is necessary during training to establish appetitive odor memories.
claims.source: In line with our findings, a very recent study suggests that KC output is necessary during training to establish appetitive odor memories (Pribbenow et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Pribbenow et al., 2022).

claims.claim: β'1 mushroom body output neurons have been implicated in courtship conditioning in Drosophila males.
claims.source: Notably, β'1 MBONs have been implicated previously in courtship conditioning in Drosophila males (Montague and Baker, 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Montague and Baker, 2016).

claims.claim: β'1 mushroom body output neurons are quite selective in their odor response.
claims.source: Our data confirms that these MBONs are quite selective in their odor response (Hige et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data and citation to previous work (Hige et al., 2015).

claims.claim: β'2 dopaminergic neurons are directly connected to MBON-β'1.
claims.source: EM connectomics and trans-TANGO data suggest that β'2 DANs are directly and β'2 MBONs indirectly connected to MBON-β'1.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by EM connectomics and trans-TANGO data.

claims.claim: β'2 mushroom body output neurons are indirectly connected to MBON-β'1.
claims.source: EM connectomics and trans-TANGO data suggest that β'2 DANs are directly and β'2 MBONs indirectly connected to MBON-β'1.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by EM connectomics and trans-TANGO data.

claims.claim: The role of the β'1 compartment is complex and bidirectional, possibly with subtypes of β'1-innervating dopaminergic neurons that connect to different downstream neurons.
claims.source: It is also conceivable that, as the behavioral data indicates, the role of the β'1 compartment is complex and bidirectional, possibly with subtypes of β'1-innervating DANs that connect to different downstream neurons and receive different inputs (see also Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1H-J).
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation based on the experimental data.

claims.claim: Mating could affect subtypes of β'1-innervating dopaminergic neurons differently such that a difference is difficult to identify at the current resolution of split-Gal4 lines.
claims.source: Mating could affect these subtypes differently such that a difference is difficult to identify at the current resolution of split-Gal4 lines.
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculative explanation for the lack of observed changes in calcium imaging.

claims.claim: State-dependent changes in the mushroom body network are relayed to the lateral horn to modulate odor attraction.
claims.source: As our data suggests, these neurons appear to undergo longer lasting changes in their response to putrescine upon mating (see Figure 7). While AD1b2 neurons in virgins do not respond differently to the water control as compared to putrescine, mated females do. Given that these neurons are involved in the expression of polyamine attraction, we favor a model where state-dependent changes in the MB network are relayed to the LH to modulate odor attraction.
claims.evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on the experimental data presented in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Mating does not induce a strong global change in brain state in female flies.
claims.source: Our in vivo whole brain imaging data suggests that, at least in female flies, mating does not induce a strong global change in brain state.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the whole brain lightfield imaging data.

claims.claim: Mating appears to induce discrete changes in a dopamine-gated learning circuit.
claims.source: Rather, mating appears to induce discrete changes in a dopamine-gated learning circuit.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on all the experimental data presented in the study.

claims.claim: Mating and sex peptide receptor signaling enhance mushroom body-dependent long-term memory in Drosophila females.
claims.source: In line with this interpretation, mating and SPR signaling were recently shown to enhance MB-dependent long-term memory in Drosophila females (Scheunemann et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Scheunemann et al., 2019).

claims.claim: A discrete signal rather than the physiological state change itself induces the observed increase in olfactory preference.
claims.source: Our data provides some evidence that a discrete signal (e.g. pheromone, the act of courting and mating) rather than the physiological state change itself induces the observed increase in olfactory preference.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claims.claim: A combination of discrete signals and systemic physiological changes work hand-in-hand or in parallel to promote the right behavior at the right time.
claims.source: Given the variety of behavioral adaptations and their ethological importance, it is conceivable that a combination of discrete signals and systemic physiological changes, possibly dependent on the type of behavioral change, work hand-in-hand or in parallel to promote the right behavior at the right time.
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculative proposal based on the experimental findings.

claims.claim: Other mating-induced adaptations in sensory perception might use the same or similar mechanism as described for polyamines.
claims.source: While not all odor responses or odor-induced behaviors are subject to mating-induced changes, it is conceivable that other mating-induced adaptations in sensory including odor perception use the same or similar mechanism as described here on the example of polyamines.
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculative proposal based on the experimental findings.

claims.claim: Odor responses in higher brain centers show relatively little odor selectivity for a specific odorant.
claims.source: Importantly, odor responses in higher brain centers show relatively little odor selectivity for a specific odorant (Frechter et al., 2019; Hige et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Frechter et al., 2019; Hige et al., 2015).

claims.claim: Mushroom body output neurons and lateral horn neurons usually respond to subgroups of odorants possibly depending on their innate or experience-dependent valence.
claims.source: MBONs and LH neurons usually respond to subgroups of odorants possibly depending on their innate or experience-dependent valence.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the response properties of these neurons.

claims.claim: The described mechanism could be a more general one allowing the responses to other odors or possibly even other sensory modalities to adapt upon mating.
claims.source: We speculate that the described mechanism could be a more general one allowing the responses to other odors or possibly even other sensory modalities to adapt upon mating.
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculative proposal based on the experimental findings.

claims.claim: The neuropeptide oxytocin induces lasting changes in the mother's cortex, transforming weaker responses to pup calls in the virgin to strong responses in mothers.
claims.source: For instance, the neuropeptide oxytocin, which is released during birth and lactation, induces lasting changes in the mother's cortex, transforming weaker responses to pup calls in the virgin to strong responses in mothers (Marlin et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Marlin et al., 2015).

claims.claim: The orchestration of internal state-dependent sensory tuning with plasticity of neurons in higher brain centers could ensure that animals remember the most relevant information at key turning points in their lives.
claims.source: The orchestration of internal state-dependent sensory tuning with plasticity of neurons in higher brain centers could, thus, ensure that animals remember the most relevant information at key turning points in their lives.
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculative proposal based on the experimental findings and broader biological context.

results.result: Mated female Drosophila show increased attraction to polyamine odors that lasts for at least 9 days after mating, while the neuromodulation of polyamine-sensitive olfactory sensory neurons declines within hours after mating.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 are well-supported by experimental data (Figure 1A, B) and citations to previous work (Hussain et al., 2016a). The temporal dissociation between short-term OSN modulation and long-lasting behavioral change is clearly demonstrated and forms the basis for investigating higher-order mechanisms.

results.result: Mating does not significantly increase female attraction to ammonia or vinegar odors.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C5 are supported by experimental data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B), demonstrating specificity of the mating-induced behavioral change to polyamines rather than a general increase in odor attraction.

results.result: Sex peptide, seminal fluid, and sperm are not essential for inducing postmating polyamine preference.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C8 are supported by experimental data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D) and citations to previous work. The experiments with SP mutant males, seminal fluid-deficient males, and sperm-deficient males all show normal polyamine preference increases, indicating these factors are dispensable.

results.result: Courtship without mating induces intermediate preference levels in virgin females.
results.evaluation: Claim C9 is supported by data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) showing intermediate behavior, but the result is not statistically significant compared to either virgins or mated females. This suggests courtship signals may contribute but is not conclusive.

results.result: Pheromone detection via ORCO-expressing olfactory sensory neurons during mating is required for the mating-induced increase in polyamine preference, but cVA alone is insufficient.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C14 are well-supported by experimental data (Figures 1C-E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G) and citations. ORCO mutants show reduced preference, blocking ORCO or OR67d OSNs during mating reduces preference, but cVA exposure alone does not induce the behavioral change. This demonstrates necessity but not sufficiency of pheromone signaling.

results.result: Standard fly food contains high levels of polyamines, with approximately 20 mg per 100 g food.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C16 are supported by chemical analysis data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F) using LC-MS/MS with stable isotope dilution. The quantification is rigorous and provides important context for the biological relevance of polyamine detection.

results.result: Kenyon cell synaptic output is required both during mating to induce the behavioral change and during the choice test to express polyamine preference.
results.evaluation: Claims C17, C18, and C84 are supported by temporal shibire experiments (Figure 2B, C). Blocking KC output during mating prevents the behavioral switch, while blocking during test reduces preference expression. Controls show that long-term inhibition per se does not affect behavior.

results.result: Mating does not induce a significant global change in brain state in female Drosophila.
results.evaluation: Claims C19 and C124 are supported by whole-brain lightfield imaging data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-E) showing no significant brain-wide or region-specific differences between virgin and mated females. This suggests discrete circuit-level changes rather than global state changes.

results.result: PAM-β'1,γ3/4 dopaminergic neurons bidirectionally modulate female polyamine preference: activation in virgins increases preference, activation during mating in mated females decreases preference, but inhibition during mating has no effect.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C23 are supported by dTrpA1 activation and shibire inhibition experiments (Figure 3A, C). The bidirectional effect is striking and well-demonstrated, though the lack of effect with inhibition suggests redundancy with other systems.

results.result: PAM dopaminergic neurons promote expression of mated female odor attraction, while PPL1 dopaminergic neurons suppress expression of odor attraction in virgins.
results.evaluation: Claims C24, C25, C85, and C86 are supported by shibire experiments at test (Figure 3—figure supplements 1A, B and 2A-H). The opposing roles of PAM and PPL1 DANs in expression of preference are clearly demonstrated and provide insight into state-dependent circuit regulation.

results.result: MBON-β'1 synaptic output during mating is required for induction of mating-related behavioral changes, and activation in virgins is sufficient to increase polyamine preference.
results.evaluation: Claims C26, C27, and C87 are supported by shibire inhibition and dTrpA1 activation experiments (Figure 4A, B). The necessity during mating and sufficiency in virgins strongly implicate MBON-β'1 in the induction phase of the behavioral change.

results.result: MBON-β'1 activation at the time of choice bidirectionally modulates polyamine attraction in virgins and mated females, but inhibition at test does not significantly alter preference.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C30 are supported by experimental data (Figure 4—figure supplements 1B, C and 2A). The bidirectional effect with activation but lack of effect with inhibition suggests complex regulation, possibly involving compensatory mechanisms.

results.result: PAM-β'2m dopaminergic neurons receive direct input from MBON-β'1, and β'2 MBONs are indirectly connected to MBON-β'1, suggesting a recurrent circuit.
results.evaluation: Claims C31, C119, and C120 are supported by trans-TANGO experiments and EM connectome data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E-G). The anatomical connectivity provides a structural basis for understanding the functional interactions between β'1 and β'2 compartments.

results.result: MBON-β'2 output is required for expression of polyamine preference in mated females but not for induction of the mating-induced behavioral change.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C34, C89, C90, and C92 are supported by dTrpA1 activation and shibire inhibition experiments (Figure 4D, E, Figure 4—figure supplements 1D and 2B). The temporal specificity (required at test but not during mating) distinguishes β'2 from β'1 function.

results.result: Polyamine-detecting olfactory sensory neurons express IR76b and IR41a, and putrescine stimulation activates neurons primarily in the ventral lateral horn while vinegar activates dorsal lateral horn neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C37 are supported by citations and lightfield imaging data (Figure 5A). The spatial segregation of odor responses in the lateral horn provides a basis for identifying relevant output neurons.

results.result: AD1b2 lateral horn output neurons receive direct input from VC5 projection neurons and provide input to the β'1 mushroom body compartment; inhibition of AD1b2 output during test reduces mated female attraction to putrescine.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C40 are supported by EM connectome data and behavioral experiments with multiple Gal4 lines (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, H). The convergence of anatomical and functional evidence strongly implicates AD1b2 in polyamine attraction.

results.result: aSP-g lateral horn output neurons receive input from the DA1 glomerulus (cVA-responsive) and their inhibition reduces mated female attraction to putrescine.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C42 are supported by EM connectome data and behavioral experiments (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D). This provides a link between pheromone detection and polyamine preference expression.

results.result: MBON-β'1 responds to cVA but not putrescine, and mating does not lead to long-lasting modulation of this response.
results.evaluation: Claims C43, C44, and C95 are supported by calcium imaging data (Figure 6A-E). The odor selectivity confirms the role of β'1 in processing mating-related signals, but the lack of long-lasting modulation suggests plasticity may occur elsewhere or at different timescales.

results.result: MBON-β'2 responds equally to putrescine and cVA, and mating does not induce long-lasting modulation of polyamine response.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C46 are supported by calcium imaging data (Figure 6F-H). The broad odor tuning and lack of long-lasting modulation suggest β'2 MBONs may be modulated acutely or that plasticity occurs downstream.

results.result: Optogenetic activation of PAM β'1,γ3/4 dopaminergic neurons leads to activation of β'1 and β'2 mushroom body output neurons.
results.evaluation: Claim C47 is supported by calcium imaging with optogenetic stimulation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, C). This suggests excitatory connections between these DANs and MBONs in addition to neuromodulatory effects.

results.result: AD1b2 lateral horn neurons show mating-induced lasting modulation: they respond equally to water and putrescine in virgins but respond significantly stronger to putrescine in mated females.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C50 and C99 are supported by calcium imaging data (Figure 7). This is a key finding showing that lasting plasticity occurs in the lateral horn, providing a mechanism for the persistent behavioral change.

results.result: MBON-α2sc, which connects the mushroom body to the lateral horn, is required for expression of polyamine attraction in mated females.
results.evaluation: Claims C51 and C100 are supported by shibire experiments (Figure 7—figure supplement 1). This provides evidence for a pathway by which MB modulation could be relayed to the LH.

results.result: Mating-related sensory experience regulates female odor perception and expression of choice behavior through a dopamine-gated learning circuit involving β'1 compartment for induction and β'2 compartment and lateral horn for expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C55, C75-C79, and C125 represent the main conclusion synthesizing all experimental findings. The model is well-supported by converging evidence from behavioral, imaging, and connectomics experiments showing discrete circuit-level changes rather than global brain state changes.

results.result: Courtship-promoting signals such as cVA contribute to the switch in preference behavior during mating, but the presence of food odor during mating is not required.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C83 are supported by experiments blocking ORCO OSNs during mating and mating on agarose or holidic diet (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1H, I). This demonstrates the importance of pheromone detection but not food odor presence during mating.

results.result: At the time of mating, MBON-β'1 and dopaminergic neurons innervating the β'1 compartment modulate polyamine attraction, with the β'1 compartment providing a contextual signal conveyed to the mushroom body through mating experience.
results.evaluation: Claims C88 and C91 are supported by the combined behavioral and imaging data showing the role of β'1 during mating. The model is consistent with learning paradigms where DANs provide contextual signals.

results.result: Multiple lateral horn output neurons including AD1b2 and aSP-g are involved in mated female attraction to polyamines.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C94 are supported by behavioral screens with multiple Gal4 lines and connectomics data (Figure 5D, citations). The involvement of multiple LHONs suggests distributed processing of polyamine attraction.

results.result: The lack of observed long-lasting changes in MBON odor responses could be due to transient plasticity, complex bidirectional modulation, or plasticity in downstream neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C98 and C122 are speculative explanations for negative results. While plausible, these hypotheses require additional experiments to test. The speculation is reasonable given the complexity of the circuit.

results.result: PAM-β'1,γ3/4 is sufficient but not strictly necessary for inducing mated-like behavior in virgins, suggesting multiple parallel systems ensure the transition from virgin to mated state.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C114 are supported by the activation and inhibition experiments (Figure 3A, C). The sufficiency without necessity indicates redundancy, which is biologically reasonable for an important reproductive behavior.

results.result: State-dependent changes in the mushroom body network are relayed to the lateral horn to modulate odor attraction.
results.evaluation: Claim C123 is supported by the combined evidence from MB manipulations, MBON-α2sc experiments, and AD1b2 imaging (Figures 4, 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1). This model integrates the MB and LH findings into a coherent framework.

results.result: A discrete signal rather than physiological state change itself induces the observed increase in olfactory preference, though multiple signals and physiological changes may work in parallel.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C128 are supported by experiments with sterile males, ovoD mutants, and DAN activation (Figures 1, 3). The evidence favors discrete signals but acknowledges the likely complexity of the actual mechanism.

results.result: The described mechanism could apply to other mating-induced adaptations in sensory perception and choice behaviors beyond polyamines.
results.evaluation: Claims C129, C132, and C81 are speculative proposals based on the broad odor tuning of MBONs and LHONs. While plausible, this generalization requires experimental validation with other odors and behaviors.
